In this task, participants were asked to report a briefly presented probe at the location of one of the previously presented search items.

With short intervals, participants responded faster to probes presented at locations that matched cued distractor features, indicating initial attention deployment to those features, even when they characterized the distractors participants were instructed to ignore.

Adopting a conservative effect size (Cohen's d =.60) for this specific comparison, based on the negative cueing benefit reported by Zhang and Carlisle (2023), this analysis indicated that 24 participants were required to detect the negative cueing benefit with 80% power (alpha level = .050).

table.text: Accordingly, we recruited 24 volunteers (16 female, 8 male; age: 23.46±3.05 years).
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, as verified by visual acuity and color vision screening with an OCULUS Binoptometer 3 (OCULUS Optikgeräte GmbH, Wetzlar, Germany).
All participants provided written informed consent prior to the experiment and were compensated with course credits or 9 € per hour.
Participants were seated in front of a 22-inch VPixx VIEWPixx monitor (Vpixx Technologies Inc.) at a viewing distance of approximately 100 cm.
Participants were asked to search through either four (easy search) or eight (difficult search) colored Gabor patches to find the target.
Participants had the chance to take a rest after having finished half of the block or the entire block.
In contrast, the benefits from negative cues were conditional, emerging only in the difficult search, where participants had to search through 8 colored items.
All participants provided written informed consent and were compensated with course credits or payment of €10 per hour.
Specifically, participants completed eight blocks with negative cues and seven blocks each for positive and neutral cues, with block order randomized across participants.

Using steady-state potentials to track feature-selective processing in early visual cortex, Jänig et al. (2026) found that the cued color was rapidly facilitated after the cue, irrespective of whether participants were instructed to attend to it or to ignore it.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: The sample size for this study was determined a priori via G*power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2009), targeting the RT difference between negative and neutral cues in the difficult search condition, tested via a two-tailed paired t test. Adopting a conservative effect size (Cohen's d =.60) for this specific comparison, based on the negative cueing benefit reported by Zhang and Carlisle (2023), this analysis indicated that 24 participants were required to detect the negative cueing benefit with 80% power (alpha level = .050). Accordingly, we recruited 24 volunteers (16 female, 8 male; age: 23.46±3.05 years).

Combining the two experiments, the effect size of negative cueing benefits in the difficult search was dz = 0.30 (95% CI [0.02, 0.57]), which is smaller than in Experiment 1 alone. For an effect of this size, a sample of 30 would detect it with a power of only about 36%, so a non-significant result in Experiment 2 is not surprising. Besides, behavioral responses in Experiment 2 were numerically slower than in Experiment 1 by a similar amount with positive cues (22 ms) and neutral cues (25 ms), but by about twice as much with negative cues (52 ms). The missing cueing benefit thus reflected relatively slower responses with negative cues, and not faster responses with neutral cues. The experiments also differed in context, as easy and difficult trials were intermixed in Experiment 1 whereas Experiment 2 contained only difficult trials, and we cannot determine whether this difference contributed. Whatever its source, our EEG results describe how the cues were processed in a sample in which negative cues did not speed responses, and they cannot show how the benefit observed in Experiment 1 arises. 4.4 Conclusion Knowing in advance which color to ignore can make visual search faster, but the benefit appears small and dependent on search difficulty. In the experiment with EEG, in which negative cues did not speed responses, we found no evidence for preemptive suppression, as alpha lateralization before the search display did not differ between negative and neutral cues, and the early positivity was modulated similarly for positively cued targets and negatively cued distractors.

live_data_statements: In this task, participants were asked to report a briefly presented probe at the location of one of the previously presented search items.

With short intervals, participants responded faster to probes presented at locations that matched cued distractor features, indicating initial attention deployment to those features, even when they characterized the distractors participants were instructed to ignore.

Adopting a conservative effect size (Cohen's d =.60) for this specific comparison, based on the negative cueing benefit reported by Zhang and Carlisle (2023), this analysis indicated that 24 participants were required to detect the negative cueing benefit with 80% power (alpha level = .050).
Accordingly, we recruited 24 volunteers (16 female, 8 male; age: 23.46±3.05 years).
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, as verified by visual acuity and color vision screening with an OCULUS Binoptometer 3 (OCULUS Optikgeräte GmbH, Wetzlar, Germany).
All participants provided written informed consent prior to the experiment and were compensated with course credits or 9 € per hour.
Participants were seated in front of a 22-inch VPixx VIEWPixx monitor (Vpixx Technologies Inc.) at a viewing distance of approximately 100 cm.
Participants were asked to search through either four (easy search) or eight (difficult search) colored Gabor patches to find the target.
Participants had the chance to take a rest after having finished half of the block or the entire block.
In contrast, the benefits from negative cues were conditional, emerging only in the difficult search, where participants had to search through 8 colored items.
All participants provided written informed consent and were compensated with course credits or payment of €10 per hour.
Specifically, participants completed eight blocks with negative cues and seven blocks each for positive and neutral cues, with block order randomized across participants.

Using steady-state potentials to track feature-selective processing in early visual cortex, Jänig et al. (2026) found that the cued color was rapidly facilitated after the cue, irrespective of whether participants were instructed to attend to it or to ignore it.

text.text: Studies examining whether knowing the color of an upcoming distractor (i.e., a negative cue) benefits performance in a subsequent search task have reported inconsistent findings.

A central question is whether negatively cued features can be preemptively suppressed (i.e., before distractors capture attention) or whether they initially capture attention and are then handled reactively (i.e., after capture).
Negative cueing benefits tend to emerge in difficult search, but neural evidence is rare.
To examine the boundary of such benefits and their neural basis, we conducted two experiments.
Experiment 1 manipulated task difficulty through the number of task-relevant items while keeping the overall set size constant.
Results showed that negative cues speeded up search responses in difficult search (8 task-relevant items) but not in easy search (4 items).
Experiment 2 recorded EEG during difficult search to reveal how negatively cued distractors are processed.
Preemptive suppression predicts a distractor positivity (P D ), without a distractor N2pc.
In contrast, reactive suppression predicts an initial distractor N2pc, followed by a P D .
Behavioral results showed that negative cues neither speeded response, nor yielded any cost.
ERP results showed that negatively cued distractor elicited a weak N2pc, and no later P D followed it.
In addition, alpha activities before the search display did not differ between negative and neutral cues.
We therefore found no evidence for either preemptive or reactive suppression of the negatively cued distractors, leaving open whether benefits of negative cues rely on suppression.
Visual search is often guided by explicit goals held in working memory (Folk et al., 1992; Gaspelin & Luck, 2018; Wolfe, 2021; Yu et al., 2023).

However, empirical findings on this topic remain inconsistent, and its underlying mechanisms require further clarification (Carlisle, 2023; Chelazzi et al., 2019).

text.text: 1.1 Hypotheses about distractor handling Two major hypotheses have been proposed to account for cue-guided rejection.

The "search and destroy" hypothesis posits that attention first goes to cued distractor features before they can be successfully ignored (Moher & Egeth, 2012), leading to a two-stage process (search and destroy).
text.formatted: The "search and destroy" hypothesis posits that attention first goes to cued distractor features before they can be successfully ignored <ref type="bibr">(Moher & Egeth, 2012)</ref>, leading to a two-stage process (search and destroy).

text.text: Evidence supporting this view derives from several studies.
Moher and Egeth (2012), for instance, combined a cued search task with a probe-dot detection task that had to be performed on some trials.
text.formatted: Moher and Egeth <ref type="bibr">(2012)</ref>, for instance, combined a cued search task with a probe-dot detection task that had to be performed on some trials.

text.text: In this task, participants were asked to report a briefly presented probe at the location of one of the previously presented search items.
By varying the time interval between the search display and the onset of the probe, the authors were able to track attentional allocation over time.

With short intervals, participants responded faster to probes presented at locations that matched cued distractor features, indicating initial attention deployment to those features, even when they characterized the distractors participants were instructed to ignore.
With longer intervals, however, probes at these locations produced slower responses, indicating successful ignoring at a later period.

Follow-up eye-tracking studies revealed that participants' initial fixations landed more often on items matching the cued distractor features, whereas subsequent fixations were less likely than expected by chance (Beck et al., 2018).

text.text: These findings provide direct support for the "search and destroy" hypothesis.

Conversely, the "preemptive suppression" hypothesis posits that cued distractor features can be suppressed without initially attending to them (Carlisle, 2023; Carlisle & Nitka, 2019; Zhang et al., 2020).

In other words, the negative cue is used to generate a positive color template for identifying the target.

text.text: The authors hypothesized that since the majority of trials consisted of 2S display, the attentional control settings established for these displays would generalize to the few multi-color displays.

According to the color or spatial recoding hypothesis, negative cues should facilitate search in 2S displays because participants can set up a positive template, based on either color or location, for the non-cued items.
This strategy, however, should not be transferable to MI displays, where participants would be unable to use the negative cue to generate a positive color or spatial template.

Contrary to this prediction, their results revealed a negative cueing benefit even in the multi-color displays (MS and MI), leading the authors to conclude that neither color nor spatial recoding can fully explain the observed negative cueing benefits.
Alongside the debate, a clear consensus on the neural mechanisms remains elusive.

1.5 Rationale Existing EEG studies on negative cues face two key limitations that constrain our understanding of the mechanisms underlying cue-guided distractor handling.
First, too simple search task reduced participants' incentive to use negative cues.
Second, negative cueing benefits are often confounded by learned suppression, making it difficult to isolate the unique contribution of negative cues during visual search.

To resolve these limits, the search displays used in the present study contained either 4 (easy) or 8 (difficult) task-relevant (colored) items, presented alongside several task-irrelevant gray items, keeping the overall set size constant while varying the difficulty of the search task.
Each search display was preceded by either a positive, a negative or a neutral cue.

Crucially, the color cues were laterally presented and the cued colors varied on a trial-by-trial basis rather than being fixed, thereby minimizing the possibility of participants carrying over the information from previous trials.
Based on this design, we hypothesized that if participants can effectively use negative cues, their responses should be faster in trials preceded by negative cues compared to neutral cues.

Conversely, if they cannot use negative cues effectively, responses should be comparable to those following neutral cues (replicating the findings of Arita and colleagues, 2012, with small set sizes) or even slower (as observed by Berggren and Eimer, 2021).

text.text: Furthermore, we predicted that participants would be more likely to rely on negative cues in the difficult search (8 task-relevant items) than in the easy search (4 task-relevant items), because the increased attentional demands would make negative cue use more valuable.
To preview the results from Experiment 1, we observed that negative cues led to faster responses than neutral cues, but only in difficult search.
Experiment 2 therefore focused on the difficult task and recorded EEG to ask whether neural signals provide evidence for preemptive or reactive suppression.

As the position of the cue was unrelated to where targets and distractors would later appear, this lateralization cannot reflect preparation for an expected location.

Higher alpha power over a hemisphere is taken to reflect inhibition of processing in that hemisphere (Foxe & Snyder, 2011), so more positive lateralization, defined as relatively higher alpha power contralateral to the cue, would indicate that the cue and the color it carries were processed less.

If cued distractor colors were suppressed before search display onset, alpha lateralization in the cuesearch task interval should be more positive after negative than after neutral cues.
In contrast, if cued target colors were selected in advance, alpha lateralization should be more negative after positive than after neutral cues.
2 Experiment 1 2.1 Methods

The sample size for this study was determined a priori via G*power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2009), targeting the RT difference between negative and neutral cues in the difficult search condition, tested via a two-tailed paired t test.

text.text: Accordingly, we recruited 24 volunteers (16 female, 8 male; age: 23.46±3.05 years).
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, as verified by visual acuity and color vision screening with an OCULUS Binoptometer 3 (OCULUS Optikgeräte GmbH, Wetzlar, Germany).
All participants provided written informed consent prior to the experiment and were compensated with course credits or 9 € per hour.

The experimental procedure was approved by the ethics committee of the Department of Psychology at Philipps-Universität Marburg (No. 2021-56k), and conducted in accordance with the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki.
The experiment took place in a dimly lit, electricity-shielding room.
Participants were seated in front of a 22-inch VPixx VIEWPixx monitor (Vpixx Technologies Inc.) at a viewing distance of approximately 100 cm.
The experiment was controlled by a Windows 7 computer (1680*1050 pixel screen resolution, 60-Hz refresh rate) using E-prime 2.0 software.
All stimuli were presented on a black (0.28cd/m2) background.

Gabor patches (with a radius of 0.81° visual angle, cosine envelope, frequency of 0.05 and deviation of 12 pixels) were generated via the online Gabor-patch generator (https://www.cogsci.nl/gabor-generator).

text.text: They were displayed in one of four isoluminant colors (red [R:199, G:0, B:0], 18.83cd/m2; green [R:0, G:103, B:0], 18.45cd/m2; blue [R:0, G:84, B:159], 18.99cd/m2; gray [R:80, G:80, B:80], 19.09cd/m2) and tilted to one of four orientations (0°, 90° and ±15° relative to vertical midline).
Each search display consisted of gray Gabor patches and patches of another two colors that were randomly chosen for each trial.
Gabor patches with gray color were always task-irrelevant; they could be any of the four orientations.

The Gabor patches with non-gray colors were task-relevant; only one of them contained a target orientation that was tilted to the left (-15° relative to vertical midline) or right (+15° relative to vertical midline), whereas the others were oriented either 0° or 90° to prevent the target orientation from popping out.
The proportion of vertical Gabor patches was matched across task difficulties at 50% for both target-and distractor-colored items in each condition.

Each display contained 24 Gabor patches with 4, 8 and 12 Gabor patches on an inner (radius: 2.42°), middle (radius: 4.84°) and outer (radius: 7.26°) imaginary circle; Gabor patches were spaced equally on each imaginary circle.
The target was never presented on the outer circle, but at every other candidate location with equal probability, independent of task difficulty.

Task difficulty was manipulated by increasing the number of colored Gabor patches from 4 to 8 items (see Fig. 1A for an example), based on the finding that negative cues demonstrated a RT benefit at set size 8 but not at set size 4 (Arita et al., 2012).  which the task-relevant color cue appeared.

text.text: After a short delay, either a positive, a negative or a neutral cue was presented for 250 ms.

After another delay, the search display was shown, which required participants to detect an orientation target (highlighted with a dashed white circle) and report whether its orientation was tilted to the left or right.
As shown in Fig. 1C, each trial started with a central fixation point and two arrow cues, indicating the side on which the task-relevant color cue appeared.

text.text: After a randomized delay for 300-500 ms, one of three lateralized cues (positive, negative or neutral) was presented for another 250 ms.
Left/right cue positions and three task-relevant colors (red, green, blue) were fully counterbalanced within each condition and presented in a random order across the whole experiment.
After another randomized delay period for 800-1000 ms, the search display was shown.
Participants were asked to search through either four (easy search) or eight (difficult search) colored Gabor patches to find the target.
The target was a tilted non-gray Gabor patch; participants reported whether it was tilted to the left or right.
Responses were collected via a gamepad with two buttons labeling left and right.
Participants used their index or middle fingers of the right hand to press one of the buttons.
They were instructed to respond as quickly and accurately as possible.
In case of an erroneous response or a slow response (>4000 ms), a white text with "incorrect" or "too late" would appear for 500 ms on the screen.
text.formatted: In case of an erroneous response or a slow response (>4000 ms), a white text with "incorrect" or "too late" would appear for 500 ms on the screen.

text.text: Each trial was followed by a blank interval for 1000 ms.
The experiment consisted of a total of 18 blocks with 64 trials each.
Participants had the chance to take a rest after having finished half of the block or the entire block.
They also got feedback about mean accuracy and RTs after each block, lasting for 3000 ms.
The three cue types were presented in separate blocks.
Their order followed a Latin-square design and was counterbalanced across participants.
Easy and difficult search trials were randomly intermixed within the block.
Participants practiced at least one block for each cue type prior to the experimental blocks.
The experiment started when mean accuracy was above 65% and mean RTs below 4000 ms.
We focused our analysis on RTs.
Trials with responses faster than 200 ms or slower than 4000 ms were excluded.
Incorrect trials (shown in Table 1) and trials in which RTs exceeded ± 2.5 SD from the condition-specific mean were removed.

text.text: A two-way repeated-measures ANOVA was conducted on the remaining RTs, with cue type (positive, negative, neutral) and task difficulty (easy, difficult) as within-subject factors.
All statistical analyses reported here were performed with JASP 0.18.3 (JASP Team, 2024).
Degrees of freedom and p values were Greenhouse-Geisser corrected for violations of sphericity.
Planned contrasts compared positive and negative cues with neutral cues within each search difficulty using paired t tests, and p values were Holm-corrected among four tests.

Results clearly revealed the differential effects of positive and negative cues across task difficulties.
The beneficial effects of positive cues were general, appearing in both easy and difficult searches.
In contrast, the benefits from negative cues were conditional, emerging only in the difficult search, where participants had to search through 8 colored items.
This finding aligns well with previous findings, suggesting that the effectiveness of negative cues increases with search difficulty (Arita et al., 2012; Conci et al., 2019).

text.text: Crucially, a key feature of our design was that the total number of items (the overall set size) was held constant across conditions; only the number of task-relevant (colored) items varied.

Therefore, our findings provide compelling evidence that task difficulty is determined not by the overall set size, but by the number of potential target and distractor items that must be searched, at least when irrelevant items share a common feature allowing group-level rejection (Duncan & Humphreys, 1989).

text.text: Experiment 2 focused on the difficult search and recorded EEG to examine the neural signals that accompany the processing of cued distractors.
We analyzed three markers: the Pᴅ and the N2pc after search display onset, and alphaband lateralization in the cue-search task interval.
We tested two predictions coming from the preemptive suppression account which assumes that participants can use negative cues to suppress distractor features before they capture attention.
First, if suppression is prepared before the search display appears, alpha lateralization in the cue-search interval should be more positive after a negative cue than after a neutral cue.
Second, the cued distractor should elicit a P D (Gaspelin & Luck, 2018; Sawaki & Luck, 2010), and no distractor N2pc is expected.
text.formatted: Second, the cued distractor should elicit a P D <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Gaspelin & Luck, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Sawaki & Luck, 2010)</ref>, and no distractor N2pc is expected.

text.text: The "search and destroy" account, in contrast, (Moher & Egeth, 2012), assumes that the cued distractor initially captures attention before it can be suppressed, which should be reflected in a distractor N2pc, indicating attention capture, followed by a P D , reflecting reactive suppression.

text.text: A new group of thirty naive participants (21 female, 9 male, age: 22.70 ± 2.68 years) was recruited for this experiment.
All had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
Visual acuity and color vision were tested with the OCULUS Binoptometer 3 (OCULUS Optikgeräte GmbH, Wetzlar, Germany).
All participants provided written informed consent and were compensated with course credits or payment of €10 per hour.

The experimental procedure was approved by the ethics committee of the Department of Psychology at Philipps-Universität Marburg (No. 2021-56k), and conducted in accordance with the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki.
Apparatus, stimuli and procedure were largely identical to Experiment 1, with three modifications.

To keep the number of trials doable, we included only the difficult search task; this adjustment was based on the finding from Experiment 1 where negative cueing benefits were observed exclusively in this condition.
Second, to increase the statistical power for the negative cue condition, we allocated it a proportionally larger number of blocks.
Specifically, participants completed eight blocks with negative cues and seven blocks each for positive and neutral cues, with block order randomized across participants.
Lastly, the delay periods before and after color cue presentation were fixed at 400 ms and 900 ms respectively.
These durations were standardized to the mean values of randomized intervals used in Experiment 1.

This approach ensured identical timing across all three cue types, avoiding chance differences in realized delay that could arise under jittering with finite trials, at the cost of increased temporal predictability.
The criteria of trial exclusion were identical to those used in Experiment 1.
A one-way repeated measure ANOVA with the factor cue type (positive, negative, neutral) was conducted on RT results.
Degrees of freedom and p values were Greenhouse-Geisser corrected for violations of sphericity.
Follow-up contrasts compared positive and negative cues with neutral cues using paired t tests, and p values were Holm-corrected among two tests.
Bayes factors (BF01 ) were computed as described in Section 2.1.4.
Error rates are reported in Table 1.

text.text: The EEG was recorded with a BrainAmp amplifier from 64 Ag/AgCI active electrodes (actiCAP, Brain Products, Munich, Germany) placed according to the international 10-10 system.
Electrode impedances were kept below 5 kΩ.
The sampling rate was set at 1000 Hz (high cutoff: 250 Hz, low cutoff: 0.016 Hz), electrodes were online referenced to FCz.

Blinks and eye movements were monitored by deriving bipolar recordings from electrodes placed below the left eye and FP1 (vertical electrooculogram, vEOG), and from electrodes (FT9 and FT10) placed near the outer canthi of each eye (horizontal EOG, hEOG).
EEG data were processed offline, using the Fieldtrip toolbox (Oostenveld et al., 2011) and custom Matlab scripts for preprocessing.
text.formatted: EEG data were processed offline, using the Fieldtrip toolbox <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Oostenveld et al., 2011)</ref> and custom Matlab scripts for preprocessing.

text.text: The EEG signal was re-referenced to the average of the left and right mastoid, and bandpass-filtered between 1 and 35 Hz (zero-phase, two-pass 4th-order Butterworth IIR filter; effective cutoffs at half-amplitude; slope ≈ 48 dB/octave).
Continuous data was segmented into epochs ranging from 2.85 s before search display onset (equivalent to 1.05 s before the arrow cue onset) to 1.15 s after search display onset.
Trials removed in the behavioral analyses were also excluded from EEG processing.

Additional trials were discarded if they contained eye blinks (vEOG > ±75μV), or horizontal eye movements (hEOG > ±35μV) within the time window from 200 ms before to 400 ms after the search display onset.

text.text: Trials were also rejected if the voltages at PO7/PO8 exceeded ±75μV (absolute amplitude threshold) at any sample between 200 ms before and 400 ms after search display onset.
All participants retained sufficient data for analysis, with fewer than 30% of trials rejected.
On average, 89.07% of trials were artifact-free and included in the final analysis.
To analyze event-related potentials evoked by the search display, we focused on epochs ranging from 200 ms before to 500 ms after search display onset.
Epochs were baseline-corrected using a 200 ms pre-search interval.

To isolate hemisphere-specific attentional activity, we computed contralateral-minus-ipsilateral difference waveforms, separately for trials in which the target or distractor appeared in the lateral visual field.
We employed a data-driven yet theoryinformed approach to define the analysis time windows for the N2pc and Pᴅ components, following the procedure established by van Moorselaar et al. (2023).

text.text: We first identified component peaks on a grand-average difference waveform collapsed across all cue conditions (positive, negative, and neutral) and across distractor-lateral and targetlateral trials.

For the Pᴅ component, we used an 110 ms window centered on the grand-average positive peak; for the N2pc component, we used a 75 ms window centered on the grand-average negative peak (typically occurring between 200-300 ms) and calculated its mean amplitude (Berggren & Eimer, 2021; Salahub & Emrich, 2021).

Specifically mean amplitudes of original waveforms, extracted from the time windows defined above, were submitted to repeated-measure ANOVAs with the within-subject factors of cue type (positive, negative, neutral), display configuration (target lateral, distractor lateral), and laterality (contralateral, ipsilateral) to test for main effects and interactions.

text.text: Next, we tested the lateralization against zero specified by our hypotheses, with p values Holm-corrected across three tests.

A negativity was present for targets with positive cues, t(29) = -2.30, p Holm = .040, dz = -0.42, and for distractors with negative cues, t(29) = -2.46, p Holm = .040, dz = -0.45, but the Bayes factors provided only anecdotal evidence for an effect (BF01 = 0.53 and 0.40, respectively).

For targets with negative cues, the lateralization was a positive deflection and not an N2pc, t(29) = 2.83, p Holm = .028, dz = 0.52, and the Bayes factor provided moderate evidence for an effect (BF01 = 0.19).
The early positivity already differed between display configurations even under neutral cues, being larger for target-lateral displays, and this difference may persist into the later window.
The raw N2pc amplitudes may therefore also contain lateralized responses that do not relate to the cue.

To isolate the effect of the cue, we further tested whether attentional enhancement (relative to neutral cues within the same display configuration) can be triggered by informative cues using cluster-based permutation tests (10,000 permutations over 0 -500 ms, one-tailed in the direction of a negativity, clusterlevel α =.05).
These tests do not assume a predefined time window, so that effects are not missed when the conditions peak at different latencies.

Results showed a significant N2pc enhancement for target-lateral displays with positive cues (positive minus neutral) at 218 -374 ms (cluster p <.001), consistent with selection of the cued target, and a significant N2pc enhancement for distractor-lateral displays with negative cues (negative minus neutral) at 206-247 ms (cluster p = .028), consistent with capture by the cued distractor.

text.text: To describe how long such distractor capture lasted, we determined when it had fallen to 50% of its peak amplitude (offset) within the N2pc window (228-303 ms), using the jackknife method (i.e., leave-one-participant-out averages).
The enhancement of the N2pc for distractors with negative cues (negative minus neutral) peaked at 240 ms and had fallen to half of its peak by 250 ms in all 30 averages, indicating that it was brief.

For reference, the enhancement of the N2pc for targets with positive cues (positive minus neutral) peaked at 230 ms and had not fallen to half of its peak by the end of the window in 29 of the 30 averages.
The brief enhancement of distractor N2pc is compatible with a short capture of attention by the negatively cued distractors.
Reactive suppression predicts that such capture should be followed by suppression, which could be indexed by P D .

To test this, we examined the cue-related lateralization for distractors (negative minus neutral) across 250-500 ms (after the enhancement had declined), using a cluster-based permutation test (10,000 permutations, one-tailed in the direction of a positivity, cluster-level α = .05).
No positive cluster was found (see Fig. 4B), indicating no later distractor positivity.

text.text: Alpha power is a well-established index of cortical excitability, with increases reflecting inhibition and decreases reflecting facilitation of processing in the corresponding hemisphere.

Because the color cue was matched across cue types except for its central symbol, and the future position of distractors was unpredictable, any differences from neutral cues should reflect the processing of the information given by the positive or negative cue, and not suppression of a known location.

We predicted a higher alpha lateralization for negative than neutral cues if the cued distractor color was suppressed (van Zoest et al., 2021), and lower lateralization for positive than neutral cues if the cued target color was selected (de Vries et al., 2019; Foxe & Snyder, 2011).

Experiment 2 replicated the behavioral benefit of positive cues relative to neutral cues under difficult search tasks.
In contrast, negative cues did not speed responses, unlike the benefit observed in Experiment 1.
Possible reasons for this discrepancy, along with how our EEG data inform existing hypotheses, are discussed in the next section.
4 General discussion The current study investigated how prior knowledge of a distractor's color shapes visual search and how the distractor is handled.

In Experiment 1, positive cues speeded responses in both easy and difficult search, whereas negative cues speeded responses only in difficult search (with eight task-relevant items), and not in easy search (with four task-relevant items), although the total number of items was constant.

Experiment 2 replicated the benefit of positive cues but not that of negative cues in difficult search, where RT did not differ from performance seen with neutral cues (BF01 = 4.23, moderate evidence).
The EEG data provided no evidence for either preemptive or reactive suppression of negatively cued distractors.
Alpha lateralization before the search display did not differ between negative and neutral cues.
The early positivity was elicited by both lateral distractors and lateral targets.
This positivity was changed by the cue to a similar degree when the lateralized set carried the cued color, whether this set was the target or the distractor.
It therefore cannot be taken as a suppression signal.
After display onset, negatively cued distractors showed a weak N2pc, which is in line with a short capture of attention, but it was not followed by a P D .
4.1 What can the lateralized ERPs tell us about distractor handling?
In the literature, an early positivity elicited by a salient distractor has been thought to reflect preemptive suppression (Gaspelin & Luck, 2018; Sawaki & Luck, 2010).
text.formatted: In the literature, an early positivity elicited by a salient distractor has been thought to reflect preemptive suppression <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Gaspelin & Luck, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Sawaki & Luck, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In our study, negatively cued distractors also elicited an early positivity.
If this reflected preemptive suppression of a negatively cued distractor, it should be specific to distractor-lateral displays, whereas target-lateral displays should elicit little or none.
The results did not support this prediction.
Target-lateral displays elicited the early positivity as well, and it was larger than distractor-lateral displays even with neutral cues.
We thus compared the cue-related modulation, defined as the enhancement of early positivity with negative relative to neutral cues, between display configurations.
This enhancement was not significantly larger for distractor-lateral than for targetlateral displays, although this evidence was inconclusive (BF01 = 2.04).
Moreover, the enhancement of early positivity was similar for cued targets and cued distractors (BF01 = 5.00), suggesting that the positivity did not serve a function specific to distractors.

Therefore, this positivity is more likely to reflect a general priority or salience signal (Corriveau et al., 2012; Kerzel & Huynh Cong, 2023; Oxner et al., 2024 Oxner et al., , 2025)), rather than a preemptive suppression signal.
text.formatted: Therefore, this positivity is more likely to reflect a general priority or salience signal <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Corriveau et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Kerzel & Huynh Cong, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Oxner et al., 2024</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Oxner et al., , 2025))</ref>, rather than a preemptive suppression signal.

text.text: This agrees with the recent finding that a salient singleton elicits early positivity irrespective of whether it is ignored or searched for (McDonald et al., 2026).

text.text: Our evidence for equivalence is moderate, earlier inferences of preemptive suppression from this component are not refuted but should be treated with caution.
If negatively cued distractors captured attention, as the first stage of the "search and destroy" account predicts (Moher & Egeth, 2012), they should elicit an N2pc.
text.formatted: If negatively cued distractors captured attention, as the first stage of the "search and destroy" account predicts <ref type="bibr">(Moher & Egeth, 2012)</ref>, they should elicit an N2pc.

text.text: In the N2pc time window (228-303 ms), distractors with negative cues elicited only a weak negativity, supported by anecdotal evidence (BF01 = 0.40).

Considering that this raw N2pc may contain lateralized responses that do not relate to the cue, we tested the enhancement of distractor N2pc by negative cues (relative to neutral cues) using a cluster-based approach.
This test revealed a negative cluster at 206-247 ms.
Such a short effect is compatible with a brief capture of attention by the cued distractor, as a "search and destroy" account (Moher & Egeth, 2012) would predict.
text.formatted: Such a short effect is compatible with a brief capture of attention by the cued distractor, as a "search and destroy" account <ref type="bibr">(Moher & Egeth, 2012)</ref> would predict.

text.text: This account further requires that capture should be followed by suppression, but no distractor positivity followed this negativity (250-500 ms; cluster-based test).
Taken together, these results provide limited evidence that the cued distractor captured attention, and none that capture was followed by suppression.
This is consistent with views that capture is not necessarily followed by suppression (e.g., Beck et al., 2018; Hickey et al., 2006).
text.formatted: This is consistent with views that capture is not necessarily followed by suppression (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Beck et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Hickey et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, these findings provide no evidence for either preemptive suppression (Gaspelin & Luck, 2018; Sawaki & Luck, 2010) or reactive suppression (Moher & Egeth, 2012), as both require a suppression signal (P D ), and no such signal was found here.
text.formatted: Therefore, these findings provide no evidence for either preemptive suppression <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Gaspelin & Luck, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Sawaki & Luck, 2010)</ref> or reactive suppression <ref type="bibr">(Moher & Egeth, 2012)</ref>, as both require a suppression signal (P D ), and no such signal was found here.

text.text: One possible reason is that the search display did not require suppression.
In our display, target-and distractor-colored items occupied separate regions and were surrounded by uniform gray fillers, so the two groups stood out as clumps.
This may allow a clump-scanning strategy, in which attention is first directed to one group and the target is then searched for within it (Liesefeld & Müller, 2020).
text.formatted: This may allow a clump-scanning strategy, in which attention is first directed to one group and the target is then searched for within it <ref type="bibr">(Liesefeld & Müller, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Under this strategy, distractors do not compete for attention and can be ignored passively.
This would account for the absence of a distractor N2pc with positive cues ( BF01 = 3.69), and no P D specific to distractors.
Another possibility is that negative cues were recoded into a positive template (Becker et al., 2015), which would make suppression of the distractor unnecessary (e.g., Rashal et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Another possibility is that negative cues were recoded into a positive template <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Becker et al., 2015)</ref>, which would make suppression of the distractor unnecessary (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Rashal et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Because a negative cue does not tell observers which color to look for, such a template can be formed only after the search display appears, once the remaining color has been inferred.
If negative cues were recoded in this way, targets should still elicit an N2pc, but later than after positive cues.
In the N2pc window, negatively cued targets did not elicit an N2pc.
Considering that the N2pc may fall outside this window due to its delayed nature, we also checked for a later negativity.

A later negativity was present for negatively cued targets, but it was also present for targets with positive and neutral cues, for which no recoding is needed, so this late component cannot be interpreted as recoding.
We therefore found no evidence that target selection was delayed by negative cues, and our data provide no support for recoding.

One may propose that identifying the cue color on every trial automatically primes that color, irrespective of whether it later serves as the target or the distractor color (Maljkovic & Nakayama, 1994; Theeuwes, 2013).
text.formatted: One may propose that identifying the cue color on every trial automatically primes that color, irrespective of whether it later serves as the target or the distractor color <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Maljkovic & Nakayama, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Theeuwes, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Priming could therefore contribute to the effects of both positive and negative cues.
For positive cues, it makes the same prediction as strategic control, so only negative cues can be diagnostic.

Priming predicts that cues change the responses to the lateralized set carrying the cued color to the same extent for positive and negative cues, and that negative cues slow rather than speed responses, because attention would be drawn to the color that is to be ignored.
The early positivity fits the first prediction, as the enhancement of early positivity was similar for the cued target and for the cued distractor.
However, this result does not exclude strategic control, because it would produce the same pattern.
The N2pc and the behavioral results fit priming less well.

The enhancement of N2pc for distractors with negative cues was brief and had fallen to half of its peak by about 250 ms, whereas that for targets with positive cues had not by the end of the common N2pc window.
This suggests that the cue had a more lasting effect on the cued target than on the cued distractor, which is difficult to explain by a boost that is independent of the role of the cued color.
Moreover, negative cues did not slow responses in Experiment 2 ( BF01 = 4.23), and they speeded responses in Experiment 1.
A cost of priming could in principle be offset by a benefit of strategic control, in which case both mechanisms would contribute.
Therefore, priming is unlikely to be the only factor, although it may contribute to the current findings, and our data cannot separate it from strategic control.
Before the search display appeared, we asked whether the cued color was processed differently after negative cues than after neutral cues.

The color cue appeared at a lateral position that was unrelated to the positions of the distractors in the search display, so lateralized alpha could not reflect suppression of an expected distractor location.

We used the position of the color cue as a handle on its processing, because alpha lateralization is sensitive to the processing of a lateral stimulus and the cues were matched in position, size, and color distribution.
A difference from the neutral cue should therefore reflect how the color of the cue and its central symbol were processed.
Higher alpha power is taken to reflect inhibition, and lower alpha power facilitation, of processing in the corresponding hemisphere (de Vries et al., 2019; Foxe & Snyder, 2011).
text.formatted: Higher alpha power is taken to reflect inhibition, and lower alpha power facilitation, of processing in the corresponding hemisphere <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(de Vries et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Foxe & Snyder, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: If a cued distractor color was suppressed in preparation for the search, alpha lateralization should therefore have been higher after negative than after neutral cues, whereas selection of the cued target color should have lowered it after positive cues.
The data showed neither pattern.
Negative cues did not differ from neutral cues at any time point, and the decrease after positive cues, although in the predicted direction, did not reach significance (430-620 ms).
These results provide no evidence for suppression of the cued color during the interval between the cue and the search display.
The absence of modulation on alpha lateralization by negative cues can be related to recent evidence on how a cue to ignore a color affects processing of that color.

Using steady-state potentials to track feature-selective processing in early visual cortex, Jänig et al. (2026) found that the cued color was rapidly facilitated after the cue, irrespective of whether participants were instructed to attend to it or to ignore it.
text.formatted: Using steady-state potentials to track feature-selective processing in early visual cortex, <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Jänig et al. (2026)</ref> found that the cued color was rapidly facilitated after the cue, irrespective of whether participants were instructed to attend to it or to ignore it.

text.text: The authors attributed this to stimulus-driven selection of the cued color.
Such facilitation would predict lower alpha lateralization after negative than after positive cues, which we did not observe.
The paradigms differ in ways that may explain why.

In that study, three colored dot fields were superimposed at the same location and the cue matched one of them, so facilitation of the cued color could act on a stimulus that was present at the same time, and competition occurred between colors within the same receptive fields.

In our experiment, no stimulus in the cued color was present during the cue period other than the cue itself, so there was no concurrent stimulus on which such facilitation could act, and our measure indexed the processing of the cue at its position.
The two results are therefore not directly comparable.
4.3 How robust is the benefit of negative cues?

Some studies in which the distractor color changed from trial to trial have reported benefits of negative cues, and have suggested that these benefits increase with search difficulty (Arita et al., 2012; Conci et al., 2019; Zhang & Carlisle, 2023; Zhang et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Some studies in which the distractor color changed from trial to trial have reported benefits of negative cues, and have suggested that these benefits increase with search difficulty <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Arita et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Conci et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Zhang & Carlisle, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Zhang et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Experiment 1 agrees with this pattern, as negative cues speeded responses more in the difficult search, which had eight task-relevant items, than in the easy search, which had four, although the total number of items was constant.
This also suggests that negative cueing benefits depends on the number of task-relevant items.
Experiment 2, however, which contained only the difficult search, did not reproduce the benefit of negative cues (BF01 = 4.23).

The two experiments differed in whether negative cues speeded responses in the difficult search, but this difference was not statistically significant (F(1,52) = 2.34, p = .132, ηp² = 0.043) and may reflect sampling variability.
Combining the two experiments, the effect size of negative cueing benefits in the difficult search was dz = 0.30 (95% CI [0.02, 0.57]), which is smaller than in Experiment 1 alone.
For an effect of this size, a sample of 30 would detect it with a power of only about 36%, so a non-significant result in Experiment 2 is not surprising.

Besides, behavioral responses in Experiment 2 were numerically slower than in Experiment 1 by a similar amount with positive cues (22 ms) and neutral cues (25 ms), but by about twice as much with negative cues (52 ms).
The missing cueing benefit thus reflected relatively slower responses with negative cues, and not faster responses with neutral cues.

The experiments also differed in context, as easy and difficult trials were intermixed in Experiment 1 whereas Experiment 2 contained only difficult trials, and we cannot determine whether this difference contributed.

Whatever its source, our EEG results describe how the cues were processed in a sample in which negative cues did not speed responses, and they cannot show how the benefit observed in Experiment 1 arises.
4.4 Conclusion Knowing in advance which color to ignore can make visual search faster, but the benefit appears small and dependent on search difficulty.

In the experiment with EEG, in which negative cues did not speed responses, we found no evidence for preemptive suppression, as alpha lateralization before the search display did not differ between negative and neutral cues, and the early positivity was modulated similarly for positively cued targets and negatively cued distractors.

We also found no evidence for reactive suppression, because the weak, brief enhancement of N2pc by negatively cued distractors, which is compatible with a short capture of attention, was not followed by a distractor positivity.

Crucially, we then subtracted the trial-averaged evoked response (the ERP) from each single trial's broadband signals.
This step was designed to isolate non-phase-locked activity and prevent its contamination by phase-locked components.
The resulting signals from electrodes PO7/PO8 were then decomposed on a single-trial basis using Morlet wavelets.
The window width was 5 cycles and the frequency ranged from 4 to 40 Hz in a step of 0.5Hz.
After averaging trials for each cue type, we calculated the normalized alpha lateralization (8-13Hz) using the formula (contralateral -ipsilateral / contralateral + ipsilateral) х100.
This index was used because it is sensitive to attention allocated to a lateral stimulus, and the cue's position was the only spatially anchored event during the preparatory interval.

Because the cues were matched across cue types in position, size, and color distribution and differed only in their central symbol, any difference from the neutral cue should reflect differential processing of the cue, driven by the color it carries, its symbol, or both.
We thus compared alpha lateralization between each informative cue and the neutral cue (i.e., positive vs. neutral, negative vs. neutral) with cluster-based permutation tests for paired samples.

This non-parametric test (10,000 permutations, one-tailed test, significance threshold of .05) identifies clusters of contiguous time points where the difference between conditions is significant by randomly shuffling condition labels at each iteration.
